title: The Long Shadow of Osama bin Laden
author: Walden Bello
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/binladenvideo-680x506.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/09/11/the-
long-shadow-of-osama-bin-laden/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/binladenvideo-680x506.png)

Still from a videotape released by Osama bin Laden.

Social scientists often see the individual as a product of society. But never,
never underestimate the impact of personality on society. Or at least, some
personalities. The only other personality in recent history who has had as
great an impact on global developments as Donald Trump is Osama bin Laden. If
Trump is the “Napoleonic” figure of the second 15 years of the twenty-first
century—that is, one who shifts the train of history onto a different
track—bin Laden was the one who filled that role in the first 15 years. And
Trump cannot be understood without Osama.

In the TV series _The Looming Tower,_ the dramatization of events leading up
to 9/11, the audience is told that the vision of 72 virgins waiting for them
in paradise is what motivated the terrorists.

But that is only half the story. The other half, and probably the greater
half, was bin Laden’s strategic vision.

**Che Guevara and Osama bin Laden**

I don’t know if bin Laden read Ernesto “Che” Guevara. But whether or not he
did, he and Che had essentially similar strategic visions. For Che, creating
many Vietnams to disperse the forces of the U.S. empire was the vision. For
bin Laden, it was a dramatic act that would act as an accelerant to anti-U.S.
rebellion throughout the Muslim world. Both were men of action who were
determined to put their strategies to an empirical test. Che failed, cornered
and murdered in the highlands of Bolivia. Osama succeeded despite a script
that did not go according to plan.

The attack on the twin towers was a horrific act of terrorism. But a quarter
of a century since then has provided a perspective to condemn it in no
uncertain terms as an act of terror while regarding it at the same time as a
strategic masterstroke in the war against the U.S. empire.

September 11 did not quite work out the way bin Laden intended. Instead of
being inspired, most Muslims were horrified and distanced themselves from the
terrible deed. Still, he lucked out, thanks to George W. Bush and the
neoconservatives that had come to power with him in Washington in 2001. For
them, bin Laden’s attack was a god-given opportunity to teach both America’s
enemies and friends that the empire was omnipotent. Ostensibly waged to go
after the “roots of terror,” the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq were in
fact what the Romans called “exemplary wars,” and their aim was to reshape the
global strategic environment to fit Washington’s so-called unipolar status
following the demise of the Soviet Union.

Here again the personality factor becomes relevant. Disappointed with the
reluctance of his father, George H.W. Bush, to finish off Saddam Hussein
during the 1990–1991 Gulf War, Bush _fils_ initiated these invasions as the
first steps in a demarche that would eliminate the so-called rogue states,
compel greater loyalty from dependent states or supplant them with stronger
allies, and put strategic competitors, like China, on notice that they should
not even think of vying for power with the United States.

Disregarding the lessons of Vietnam and the British and Soviet debacles in
Afghanistan, the Bush administration drove the United States into two
unwinnable wars against highly motivated insurgents in the Middle East as bin
Laden watched with satisfaction, living unperturbed under the nose of an
American ally, the Pakistani military, in the peaceful garrison town of
Abbottabad. It was not exactly the scenario he had envisaged, but he was not
about to quibble if the Bush administration, owing to its drive for unipolar
hegemony, placed the United States on the road to overextension, which was,
after all, his strategic aim.

**America’s Odyssey**

What followed was a 25-year U.S. odyssey in the Middle East, with no prospect
of reaching Ithaca in sight. Succeeding George Bush as U.S. president, Barack
Obama promised to pull America out of the Middle East, but his withdrawal of
U.S. troops from Iraq was contradicted by his participation in the toppling of
the Gaddafi government in Libya, his overseeing a surge of American forces in
Afghanistan, and his expanding the covert war against Taliban targets in
Pakistan, which cost hundreds of lives that were justified as necessary
“collateral damage.”

Donald Trump rode to power partly on the strength of anti-war sentiment,
constantly reminding people during his campaign for the presidency in 2016
that his rival Hillary Clinton had voted for the invasion of Iraq in 2003 when
she was a senator. In office, however, he ended up destabilizing the Middle
East even more. There was, first of all, his unqualified support for Israel,
which led him to a major move that infuriated Arabs: the transfer of the U.S.
embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Then, when he took the United States out
of the Iran nuclear deal, he reversed the one tension-lessening achievement of
Obama, which had put effective checks on Tehran’s development of weapons-grade
uranium in return for a relaxation of economic sanctions. Finally, he gave a
blank check for weapons purchases to Saudi Arabia, enabling the benighted
kingdom to wage its cruel intervention in the civil war in Yemen.

When he decided in 2021 to withdraw from Afghanistan, President Joe Biden was
not motivated by concerns for global peace but by an urgent desire to reframe
U.S. strategy and refocus it on China, where the United States could rely on a
strategy of containment, chiefly by naval power, for which its forces were far
better geared to carry out than chasing after popular insurgents or engaging
in nation-building where the conditions did not exist for success, as in Iraq,
Afghanistan, and Syria. Obama had tried to do this with his “Pivot to Asia”
but yielded to counter-pressures from his generals to “stay the course” in the
Middle East. By the time he came to power, Biden realized that staying the
course had radically depreciated U.S. power. That he was no peacenik but a
warlord determined to achieve unchallenged U.S. military hegemony with a new
strategy would be shown in his provocative moves to bait China in the South
China Sea by sailing ships through the Taiwan Strait a few months after the
Afghanistan withdrawal.

But as was the case with Obama and Trump, extricating from the Middle East was
easier said than done. Instead of military engagement, Washington tried to
regain a modicum of control over events there by putting together a diplomatic
rapprochement among Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the smaller Arabian Gulf states
like Qatar that would supposedly stabilize the region. The Hamas offensive
into Israel in October 2023, however, blew up this plan for regional
stabilization since the Saudi government and the other reactionary Arab states
could not afford to come to a deal with Israel while the latter was
slaughtering another Arab people, the Palestinians. The United States stood
even more isolated than when it withdrew from Afghanistan over two years
earlier, condemned by the whole Arab world, indeed by the whole world, as it
provided the Israelis with weapons to commit genocide in Gaza. Meanwhile, its
rival, China, identified with the global South and promoted a peace-making
diplomacy that contrasted with Washington’s unqualified support for Israel’s
genocidal military offensive.

**No End in Sight**

Donald Trump again ran as a “peace candidate” in the 2024 elections, but upon
his assumption of power, he put himself 100 percent behind Israel’s genocidal
strategy in Gaza. His biggest strategic blunder, however, was to allow himself
to be lured by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu into bombing Iran
under the illusion that this would trigger a popular uprising. Over six months
after his decision to go to war, Trump is trapped and desperate, with the
Iranian government in control of events and unwilling to give him an exit ramp
except a dishonorable and unconditional retreat. Day by day his unpopularity
increases, leading to the great likelihood of the Republicans losing the House
of Representatives in the 2026 mid-term elections. But Trump has at least
learned one lesson from Bush II’s misadventures: never, never introduce ground
troops or you’re really toast.

So, 15 years after he was killed by U.S. Navy Seals in Abbotabad, Osama bin
Laden continues to cast his long shadow on the Middle East and US politics. As
Nelly Lahoud, the U.S. intelligence analyst who came out with the most
detailed study of inner workings of al-Qaeda under bin Laden’s direction,
conceded, “Though the 9/11 attacks turned out to be a Pyrrhic victory for al-
Qaeda, Osama still changed the world and continued to influence global
politics for nearly a decade after.” If the United States is the confused and
dazed global power that it is today—one that has been, moreover, reduced to a
dog being wagged by the Zionist tail—that is, not to an insignificant degree,
due to Osama bin Laden.

Sometimes morally condemnable deeds create what are ultimately positive
outcomes. Indeed, history which, in less secular times was called divine
providence, works in mysterious ways.
